utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome back. The first witness we are to hear, I believe, Ms. D'Ascoli is subject to protective orders. Ms. -- just give me a moment, Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon. Protective orders, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours. The next witness is K82, and he is subject to facial and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we will go for a moment, then, into closed session to enable the witness to come into court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, K82.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to speak into the microphone, K82. The interpreters are having some trouble hearing you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would like to begin by asking the Usher to hand you a piece of paper that contains your personal information. If you could just read the paper to yourself, not aloud, and let us know if the information it contains is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the witness's pseudonym sheet and that is 65 ter 2302.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender the pseudonym sheet under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received once it's been seen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1313 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: K82, in September 2006, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in this statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender K82's statement into evidence. We have prepared two versions of his statement. One that should be tendered under seal. That's 02315, and another which is the public redacted version which is 02863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The unredacted version will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1314, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the redacted version will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness in his statement refers to a number of exhibits, four in total. And in the interests of efficiency, I do in the intend to go through these documents which he has addressed in his statement. With Your Honours' leave, I propose to read out the current 65 ter numbers of this document, documents, and ask that they be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: These are 01981 and 01995. These are their current 65 ter numbers. And these documents are respectively referred to as Exhibit P1981 and P1995 in paragraph 8 of the statement. There are two other documents. They are 65 ter 2304 and 2305, and these are referred to as P2304 and P2305 respectively at paragraph 31 of the witness's statement. I ask that all four of these documents be received, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point the Defence has one simple objection to the admission of these exhibits, not for the reason that we believe that they are not authentic, but because we believe that they cannot be admitted through this witness, regardless of the fact that during the proceedings or in his statement he made reference to them. In the transcript of his statement he also said that never before had he seen these documents and that such documents were unknown to him. For that reason, I don't believe that he is the person through whom these documents can be admitted into evidence, or if the Bench thinks otherwise, please bear in mind his view of this document and the knowledge that he has about these documents, and I'm not going to definitely ask him about these matters in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, what Defence counsel says in relation to how the witness refers to the document is correct. This is set out in his statement. He is clear that he has not seen, for example, the order P1981. However, he does explain why he thinks some of the information contained in those orders correspond with the -- with his testimony. So he does provide some information in relation to two of the documents which is P1981 and P1995. And these are set out quite clearly in the relevant sections of his statement. Similarly with the two remaining documents, again he is clear as to the limited extent of his knowledge of the document, but nevertheless provides some comments in relation to them. And I would also add that Defence counsel would be able to cross-examine him on these documents if there are -- if he has concerns about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, in the view of the Chamber there is a sufficient basis to receive each one of these four. They will each in turn become exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1316, Your Honours. P1317, P1318 and P1319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the order to which Ms. Gopalan referred to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, K82, had you previously testified in this Tribunal in the case of Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al.? This was in September 2006 and March 2007.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the chance to review your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions you were asked in the Milutinovic et al. trial today, would you provide substantially the same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Of course I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender K82's testimony in the Milutinovic et al. case. There are two versions. One is the unredacted, that's 65 ter 5205; and the redacted version is 5205.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will each be received. The unredacted version, does it need to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It will be received under seal and the other not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the unredacted version will become Exhibit P1320 under seal, and the redacted version will be Exhibit P1321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we move on, the Court Officer has drawn my attention to the fact that in the transcript at page 5, line 13, Mr. Popovic's name has not been correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I move on to the witness's in-court summary, Your Honours. The witness is a former member of the VJ brigade. His brigade's area of responsibility was in the environs of Prizren, Suva Reka, and Orahovac, and the Dragas areas. The witness describes different operations in Kosovo that his unit was involved in prior to and during the 1999 conflict. He also speaks about the PJP presence or the presence of some PJP units during some of these operations. During these operations, when conducting house-to-house searches, members of the witness's unit killed civilians, looted and burned down houses. He states that he was ordered to do so by his sergeant. During one of these operations, he participated in killing women and children who were gathered in a yard. The witness was also involved in transporting and burying bodies of victims killed during these operations. He was not punished for these crimes. End of the in-court summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: K82, as you know, your statement and testimony is before this Trial Chamber, therefore I just have a few clarificatory questions for you in relation to your evidence. Now, let's begin with your military service. You speak about this in your statement. You say that you started your military service in Senta, Vojvodina. How old were you then, K82?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I was 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how long did you commence your training for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: My training lasted three months, and I stayed in Senta until September, which is nearly six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you know how long your training should have been?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Our training basically lasted six months, but this was an accelerated procedure. One part of the unit was transferred, and we remained there until September.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in September, and I presume this is 1998 as you say in your statement, where were you sent to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They sent us from Senta to Prizren. Only some of the elements of the unit, some went to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is partly inaudible. We are very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we must draw attention to a technical problem. The interpreter is not -- no, no, the Court Officer, could you listen to me a moment, please. The interpreter is not hearing the witness. The Chamber is hearing the witness so loudly that the Chamber cannot hear the interpreter. So there is some difficulty in the connection to the interpreter from the microphone of the witness. If attention could be given to that technical problem. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Djordjevic has just told me that he cannot hear the witness as well. Therefore, I assume that has do with the same problems that you are facing as well as the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We seem to have the opposite problem. We have too loud, and the people who need to hear his original speech hear too little. We will press on as well as we can while attention is given to that, but if it becomes impossible for the interpreter to hear, it will be, of course, necessary to stop. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Witness, when we stopped off, you said that you were sent from Senta to Prizren. Could you tell us which VJ unit you joined in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We joined the 549th Motorised Brigade in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And within this brigade, which company were you attached to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We were with the technical company.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And as a member of the technical company, K82, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Our duties were to provide duty service, guard service, maintenance of trucks, workshop, and other jobs around the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I now have some questions about the uniforms you wore during your time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If I could call up P336, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: K82, do you recognise the uniforms worn by the men on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where had you seen this uniform before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We had the same camouflage uniforms, only I don't know whether the hats and the insignia were the same as the ones that we see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to your insignia, where was your insignia located on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They were on our shoulders, on the arm, and on our hats. We had some kind of beret, that's how we called them, green berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could call up P327, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: K82, shortly and the screen a number of sample insignias will appear. Could you tell us once the insignias appear on the screen if you recognise any of them as being the insignias that you wore or you had on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's insignia number 3 on the screen; is that correct? That's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move on it to private session for the next series of questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: As I mentioned, this was an operation that took place in the winter of 1998. And you say that during this operation, you were ordered to pass through the village and set up an ambush beyond the village. And you were instructed or "we were instructed to shoot anyone coming down the village." This is in paragraph 5 of his statement. When you say "we were instructed to shoot anyone coming down to the village," who were you referring to, K82, when you say "we"? If you need to go to private session to provide this answer, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: You don't have to. It was we, the soldiers, who were present there who got this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When you say "we, the soldiers" are you referring to members of your company or are you referring to others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Members of our company.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And who provided this instruction to you, this instruction to shoot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: This instruction was given by our sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Was this the immediate superior who you referred to shortly above in private session, your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You also say that you were ordered by Lieutenant-Colonel Konjikovac to return to the village in the evening and expel people from houses. Could you tell us who Lieutenant-Colonel Konjikovac is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: He was deputy brigade commander. He came to the village in the evening, and he said that the military police would come to the village and escort the population out of the village and that we should come down to the village to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, did you witness the military police escorting the population out of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes. When they came, first they entered the yards in the village. A group had already set out of the village. The military police was there, and we, the troops who had come to spend the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When you say "a group had already set out of the village," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I mean the group of the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if you recall, how many villagers were in this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you the exact number. Those were the people that I saw coming out of those front houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you are not able to recall the exact number, do you recall the composition of the group, whether there were men, women, or children, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: There were men and women. They all left their houses because they had to, because we were supposed to spend the night in their houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Was this the only group of villagers who were sent out from Ljubizda Has that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what was done in that village later. It was already evening. Those people were escorted out. And what happened later down there, I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd now like to move on to another area of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am still facing the technical problem that we mentioned earlier. I'm happy to proceed, but I wondered what the situation was in terms of resolving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was about to say that at page 13, line 18, and also at line 16 and 17 we have the naming of a senior officer, which I think needs to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: This is something that I'm -- if I may just check the reference, Your Honours. This may be -- this reference to the name is something that I discussed in advance with the witness, and the understanding is that he is of such a high rank and commanding such a large number of men that the mention of his name would not directly lead to the identification of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. That can be understood if that is the witness's view. Yes, now, your own particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told that the problem you were concerned with has already been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Well, I will just press on in that case and raise the volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Witness, now moving on to the events in Jeskovo, this is the Jeskovo operation that you participated in around February 1999 in the south of Prizren. This is set out in paragraph 6 of your statement. In relation to this operation, you said that you were told by the commander that 700 soldiers and Special Police units were taking part in this operation. What I'd like to know is which commander gave you this information? And please let us know if you need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you think it would be preferable to be in private session to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this question requires it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Just before you answer it, yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that asking this question of the witness in this way is leading because it involves reading from a statement he had given in a previous case. I believe this is a way to elicit comments on what he had already said, and I believe my learned friend that in direct examination should ask questions that the witness can answer from what he can remember and what he knows about what had happened. Here we are listening to entire paragraphs being read out, and the witness is being asked to comment on who said what. I don't think this is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think there is a problem with what is happening, Mr. Popovic. The statement which is being referred to is one which is now part of the evidence in this trial. The witness has affirmed that it is -- the evidence in that statement is correct. What the prosecuting counsel is now asking is for the witness to give the identity of a person specifically referred to in the statement. That's merely getting a piece of detail that is omitted from the statement, although the witness very clearly refers to that person and that person's role. So in those circumstances, there would be no reason to interfere with the questioning. The witness has indicated, I take it, again because of the seniority of this officer, that he sees no problem in identifying him, so we will ask the witness, if he would, to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the question or shall I put it to you again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned a commander who said that 700 soldiers and Special Police units were taking part in the Jeskovo operation. My question was: What was the name of this commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That commander was the commander of our brigade, Bozidar Delic. He informed us about that operation on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where did he inform you of this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: It was at the barracks while we were at the barracks, the first day, that night, we were issued with whatever equipment and materiel we needed, and then that night around 10.00 p.m. we set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to these Special Police units mentioned, did you subsequently learn which Special Police units took part in this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Later when we got down to the village I was able to see the members of those Special Police units who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And do you know which units they were part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I only know what was written on the uniform, Special Police units, PJP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And what colour was their uniform, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I think they were blue camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And during this operation, were you able to observe the PJP's role, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They participated in the clearing of the village from what I was able to see. They were searching the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how many members of the PJP did you see participating in the searching of the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't now remember the exact number, but I saw several of them in the village itself when the operation was well under way, when half of the village was cleared already. I can't remember the total number I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was your unit's role during this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We had the same role as every other unit. After the shelling, we started clearing the village. And when that was done, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If you recall, when was the village shelled and for how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: The village was shelled that morning. I don't know exactly what time it was, but we had taken up positions around the village. Then the shelling lasted for about an hour. And then we moved towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you know had who was responsible for the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you know which units were involved in shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which units, but I know a three-barrel anti-aircraft gun was firing, and a Praga, it must have been the artillery from our unit, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. K82, in your statement you mentioned seeing around 10 dead bodies during this operation. Can you tell us where it is you saw these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know if it was exactly 10 bodies, but around that number certainly. I saw them in the village while the village was being searched. There was shooting going on, so I can't maintain that it was exactly 10. Some were closer to me, some were further away. So I was able to see some of them better, some not so good.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And were you able to observe what these bodies were clothed in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Those that I was able to see wore normal clothing. Some had black jackets.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82. I'd now like to move on to the operation in Trnje. This is on page 7 of the witness's statement. And this is an operation that took place just after the NATO bombing. And I would like to ask you about the orders you received in relation to the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we please go to private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, moving on to when you got to the main road with your unit, and I believe the sergeant who was involved of your unit asked you and your unit members to help yourselves to food and drinks in the shops on the main road. Now, could you tell us what happened then once he -- once he said this to the units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, that was when we reached the main road. We went to the right through the village where the shops were. When we came to the shops, we stopped for a while. We went into the shop. There were already some soldiers who were ahead of us, and they told us just to refresh ourselves there. After that, we went back through the village along the same road and headed towards the bridge and the meadow where those people had gone before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this incident where you helped yourselves to items in the shops in this particular village, Trnje, was this a common occurrence in other operations that you had the opportunity or were told to take items from shops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, in the actions that I personally was involved, we didn't encounter such situations. Maybe later, when civilian trucks were used, that was sometime later. But as for this, taking goods from the shops during the clearing up, that didn't happen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82. Now, I'd like to move on to the civilians by the creek, about 30 or 40 of them who were hiding by the creek, and that's at paragraph 25. Could you tell us what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: While we were moving from the village towards the civilians in the meadow, there were a few dead women lying there. Later when we crossed the bridge and headed towards them, they found shelter there near this creek, so we were asking ourselves what to do with them. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, the dead woman that you saw on your way towards the civilians who were hiding by the creek, were you able to say how they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They were killed from small arms or from automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82. Now, I'd like to ask you about events in Mamusa. And this is in paragraph 27. You say that you continued on to Mamusa from Trnje. How far away was Mamusa from Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Beyond the river where we were standing and up to these houses, I think it was approximately 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who were you with when you went to Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Our sergeant was there and a few of our soldiers, I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what happened in Mamusa, K82?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Before we set off, the anti-aircraft gun fired at the houses at the very entrance. Later on we went to those houses, set them on fire, and went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, on your way back when you were returning to Trnje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'll repeat that, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, on your way back when you were returning to Trnje, you say that you saw some old Albanian men near the village. This is in paragraph 28. And your immediate sergeant said or he called this man over who told him that he had arrived from Lesane. Could you tell us what happened to this man and the others in his group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: This man approached and said that he had just arrived there, that he didn't know anything, that he couldn't answer any questions that he was being asked, but he was simply shot dead on the spot. The rest of them we could see their cigarettes in the dark. They were running away, and we were close to the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how old was this man who was shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: He was an elderly man. I don't know exactly what age.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. K82, this operation in Trnje, for how many days did it last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: It lasted for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how many killings did you personally witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Around 20, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And during this operation, how many dead bodies did you come across?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Between 20 and 30 dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, before we leave this area which may be about to happen, there was, in respect of paragraph 25 about page 26, line 4, of the transcript a reference to the name of a lieutenant. Is that a person whose name can be safely left or should it be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In my view, it is someone who is quite closely linked to the witness and I would recommend a redaction, but we could also ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Should I go to private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, K82, you say that you returned to Trnje to collect the bodies. Now, could you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That was on the following day after the operation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what happened or what did you see when you went to the yard where the women and children had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: When we came to this yard, the bodies were no longer there, only the dead women were in the meadow and the men by the creek.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that you assumed that the PJP had taken the bodies. Why did you make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Somebody said something to that effect in the unit, one of the soldiers said that probably these units had taken them away because apparently they arrived after our departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you also mention remembering seeing the PJP on the road to Trnje. When was it you saw the PJP on this road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That was on the road while we were travelling to Trnje to collect the bodies. I didn't see them in the very village where the bodies were. I just saw them by the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what were they doing by road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. They just happened to be there. I honestly don't know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How did you know they were PJP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We recognised their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, going back to the bodies, what is it happened to the bodies that you collected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: These bodies were loaded on to a truck and then driven towards Prizren, or actually Zur which is beyond Prizren, and this is where the bodies were buried there in the area covered with bushes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who was involved in burying these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Our unit took part. We were the ones who had collected these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And do you know how it was decided where these bodies would be buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know that. We simply went, collected the body, and buried them. How it was decided and where, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: In the evening, we were billeted in this school and some announcement came that the clearing of the neighbouring village or whatever it was was to be cleared up. And on that a point they said that they had had enough, that they weren't going to do it anymore. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: specialists. He just took out his pistol, singled out these two men. He cocked the pistol, and the two men were taken to the cellar of the school where they were tied up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, K82, in relation to your involvement in the shooting in Trnje, were you ever punished for this by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Were you punished for setting fire to the haystacks or burning houses in Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, K82, why have you come forward to testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Simply for the reason of my personal reasons and the condition that I am in in the aftermath of all these events, I'm referring to my psychological condition. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82. Now, just to finish off, in the last few paragraphs of your statement, you mention allegations of robbery that were made against you, which you deny. You were convicted of robbery and sentenced and you note that you launched an appeal in 2005. And this is in paragraph 43 of the statement. Now, could you tell us what is the status of this appeal against your conviction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That was qualified as armed robbery, but I don't think that was an armed robbery. I testified during the appeal proceedings, and after an appeal was lodged, the judgement was quashed and the whole issue was referred to retrial.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you have a retrial date scheduled, K82?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: It has been scheduled three or four times. But another participant who was supposed to appear failed to appear, and his lawyer had an accident, a car accident, in the meantime. And now it's been scheduled for the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, K82.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: At this stage I have no further questions for you. Your Honours, before I sit down, I'd just like to inform the Chamber that the witness has provided us with a copy of this appeal decision quashing the initial conviction. He provided it to us yesterday, and this has been disclosed to the Defence. We have arranged for an English translation to be obtained as well. I do not seek to tender this document, but I'm merely notifying Your Honours that it exists in case you would require it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will go into public session. We are now in public. Thank you. I think it's a convenient time to have the break now, is it, Mr. Popovic. We will do that and resume at 10 minutes past 4.00. So we'll have a break now. A Court Officer will assist you during the break. And after the break, Mr. Popovic will have some questions for you. We will need to close the shutters now. And we will go into closed session for the adjournment and resume in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honours, before I begin my examination of the witness - and I did not want to interrupt Ms. Gopalan to say this before - the Defence will emphasise that all the events this witness has testified to are not cited in the indictment individually, and they are not individually described, although some of them happened in 1999. I believe the Trial Chamber will bear this in mind, and I will certainly adapt my cross-examination accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, K82 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I say to you that the indictment will govern the matters that we make decisions on. You have no need to be concerned that the Chamber will somehow make an adverse finding of guilt in your client in respect of any matter that is not the subject of a direct allegation in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness K82, my name is Aleksandar Popovic and I am a member of the Defence team for the accused Djordjevic. I am assisted by Ms. O'Leary and counsel Djordjevic. I will ask you certain questions, but before I begin as we speak the same language, first of all in order to protect your identity, wait until my question is finished and avoid overlapping, also for the benefit of the interpreters. Witness, first of all, I'd like to establish what statements you have given to date. I will read out a list and you will please confirm. You testified in the Milosevic case in September 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I think it was in September 2002. I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. The date doesn't matter, that's why I asked about the month, it was a long time ago. After that you gave another statement in September 2006 in Sarajevo and my learned friend questioned you about that today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In March 2007 you testified in the Milutinovic et al. case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have already confirmed to my learned friend that you stand by everything you stated in your statement from September, I will not ask you about that, but I will deal with your statement from September 2006 and I will adhere mainly to that. Let us begin with Senta and the beginning of your military service. Am I right in saying that from the 17th of March, 1998, until 9 September 1998 you served in Senta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So just under six months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was your military-recorded specialty, the VES as we call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: My recorded military specialty -- actually, first to get training and then I don't know what they call it nowadays, but my training was in electronics and tanks and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that your specialty was in fact infantry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your specialty was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, it's within the framework of the technical company. It had something to do with electronical equipment in trucks, electronical devices, repairing electronic devices, that's part of the classical training you get.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And while you were getting training to repair electronics in trucks and tanks, as you said, you also had at the same time infantry training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, we had regular training like every soldier: carrying a rifle, handling hand-held rocket-launchers, this traditional boot camp training, infantry training, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it right that this infantry training lasted two months and 22 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I think you are right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you completed this infantry training and after that what did you do in Senta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: In Senta I personally was assigned on jobs like mowing grass, all sorts of chores around the barracks that we had until the 9th of September. Everyone had a certain chore or task.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in your statement in paragraph 1, and also earlier today in your testimony, you said you had abridged training. What kind of abridged training was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I said that straightaway, this abridged training of two months and 22 days was the abridged version because the regular training lasted six months. And after that a number of soldiers from this 1st Company got a transfer and we remained there until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So you completed that infantry training, and after two months and 22 days you continued to mow grass, perform chores and regular tasks around the barracks, and you say it was abridged training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we were told. This training of two months and 22 days was followed by chores like mowing grass, like doing jobs in the workshop, and other sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that there was no accelerated training in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't tell you that it wasn't accelerated training because we were told it was accelerated training and that's why it lasted only two months and 22 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in Kosovo, to which unit were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We were members of the 549th Motorised Brigade. We were in the logical battalion, the technical company.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this action in Ljubizda Has, did you have any contacts with KLA members there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at that time in that village a lorry was found with military equipment in it marked KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: As we were coming into the village we saw a civilian lorry there, but what was in it, I really don't know because we just continued on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Another witness, K54, testified before this court, and in his statement, in his testimony rather, he said that when he arrived at that village there was a truck with military equipment marked KLA there. Do you allow for the possibility that what he said is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it's not correct. The lorry was there indeed by the road because we were passing through the village in our own trucks and we went to this location behind the village where we set up the blockade. What happened next, who inspected this truck and what happened, probably that person was not with us in the same location behind the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the village or walking through the village or passing through it, whatever, did anyone tell you that that was the point of smuggling fire-arms from Albania and that this area was being used by KLA members? Did you receive any such instructions, were you told anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really don't remember any such orders. I know that we set up this blockade. I know that sometimes in the distance behind the hills we heard shots. As for these other allegations, I cannot be sure and I cannot confirm them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about the villagers who were relocated from their homes, is it true that you, or rather, the military police removed them from the houses in order for you to sleep there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: In the afternoon or early evening, the lieutenant-colonel arrived and he said that we should go back to the nearest houses in the village and that the military police would come to transport the villagers from them. He didn't know what was going to happen to them. I only know that the nearest houses to us were vacated for us to be billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you stay in those houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We spent the night there and part of the next day, I think. But the next morning at daybreak we returned to our positions above the village that we had held before.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just to be precise, we are talking about a number of houses on the edge of the village, did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I'm talking about the upper row of houses. I cannot tell you exactly how many of them were. This part of the village, that much I know, had to be vacated for us to be billeted. That means vacated of persons, and that is what was done. Those people were transported by the military police, but where they took them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And when you left the houses -- first of all, let me ask you this: Do you know what happened afterwards, did the villagers come back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: As far as I can remember and as far as I was able to see from my vantage point, they didn't return until we left because we boarded the trucks the next day and went back to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite understandable that they couldn't return before you left their houses because that was exactly the purpose of their removal, for to you spend the day there. That much I understand. But am I right in saying that you actually don't know whether after your departure they returned to their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know if they returned. I don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move to the next event described in your statement, that operation in Leska [phoen]. In your statement, paragraph 6, you say that in February 1999 -- let me ask you: Are you certain about the period that you are talking about? Can you say for sure that it was February or could it be sometime before or after that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can allow for the possibility that it might have been before or after, but as far as I can recollect it was a period of about a month before the bombing started, so that would be a month before, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I tell you that this operation took place in March or precisely on the 11th of March, 1999? Does that correspond with your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I only know that it took place before the 24th of March, but when exactly it happened, whether it was in late February or early March, I cannot say. All I know is that it took place before the date that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the order for clearing up the village was issued by Colonel Delic. Can you tell us, since you quoted him as saying that he had new information indicating that the KLA were back, am I right in saying that the commander Delic's order was to clear up the Jeskovo village from KLA commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: The commander's order was such that he told us that he had information that these members were coming back, that that village had already been cleared up once, and that early next morning we were to launch this action. And he told us that one day before the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So to summarise, Commander Delic's precise order referred to clearing up the village of members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I believe that that was the commander's order because as far as I remember he had received information that they had come back to the village. Yes, I think, and it is true, if I remember correctly, when he was asked what our army was doing on the border, Are they sun bathing? And he said, Yes, we are going to do the same the next day, if we find them. That's probably the information he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay in Kosova-Metohija, did you have an opportunity to see KLA members and to see how they actually looked like, how their uniforms and weapons looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I had an opportunity for that in Rogovo. On that occasion, two of them were killed. They had bulletproof vests and small arms and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that members of the KLA were often wearing civilian clothes and they were moving around in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I didn't have such knowledge. One of them had this flak and the rest was the normal civilian uniform, and that one had a bulletproof vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Jeskovo operation that you mentioned was under the control of certain international organisations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I truly cannot say that I knew that. I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask for D003-0285.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 0225.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move to page 2 immediately, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a report compiled by the Kosovo Verification Mission dated the 11th of March, 1999. I'm going to read to you one portion of paragraph 4 on page 2, the sentence which begins with the word "Prizren." So that's paragraph 1 on page 2. And it reads as follows: "The Prizren regional centre informed that the KLA had infiltrated into Jeskovo, a previously deserted village, approximately one week ago." So, you will confirm if I'm right, can we say that this is consistent with the information that General Delic imparted on you before you set off to carry out this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know about this. I didn't know that they were monitoring the situation and they were writing reports. And as far as I can remember, he made no reference to this, and he didn't mention them observing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You are right. That was not my question. The question was not whether he had told you -- whether General Delic told you that the international mission was going to observe this action. My question was: What I read out to you from this report is almost identical to what you were told by Colonel Delic when you were launching the action, i.e., that KLA members had entered the village that had previously been abandoned, and that that took place a week before this report was compiled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he explained it nicely to us. He said that the scouts had been there and that he had all the information that I quoted earlier. And after that we went into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when you went into action, during that action did you see any KLA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I personally didn't see any KLA members during the actions. I did see, though, a few dead bodies down there in the village, but I couldn't distinguish them as members of KLA because none of them was dressed in a uniform or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We are coming to that later. According to what you know, how many dead bodies did you see? In your previous statement you said about ten, so it could be more than ten or fewer than ten? I know it's not very nice to speak about people in that way, but would you confirm what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. The number would be seven, eight, or ten as far as I was able to count in the area through which we passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in this context, can we now see D003-0227, please. Page 2, paragraph 4, I think. That's right. That's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is another report by the Kosovo Verification Mission dated the 13th of March, 1999. It speaks about the activities relating to the 12th of March. What I would like you to focus on is the passage, I think it's the fourth passage. It begins C/S 28, and it says: "Colonel Petrovic and the milicija entered into Jeskovo in order to carry out investigation into yesterday's operations in the village. Seven KLA bodies were found to the north of and on the outskirts of the village. All were dressed in black KLA uniforms and had apparently died from small-arms fire." Today -- actually my first question would be the following: Would you agree that there were seven bodies, whether they were KLA members or not we'll discuss that later, but do you agree that you may have seen seven bodies too while you were in Jeskovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I'm telling you again that I cannot confirm this with any degree of certainty. As much as I try hard to remember the number of the bodies and to come up with the figure that you mentioned, that seven, that were seen throughout the village, from the point when we entered and to the point where we exited. But I cannot tell you for sure how many bodies exactly there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your today's testimony on page 19, lines 10 to 11, you say the dead people had black jackets on when you speak about the dead people in the village of Jeskovo. Here we see that members of the Kosovo Verification Mission saw the bodies dressed in black KLA uniforms. Would you allow for the possibility that these black jackets that you yourself saw were actually the black uniforms mentioned by the international verifiers, I presume that you didn't come closer to check what was on the jackets, but please can you tell us more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with any surety because in such periods you have no time to think who it was and who was wearing what. Everything was developing so quickly. Nobody bothered to check the number of the bodies or to check the clothing. As far as I can remember, somebody probably had a black jacket, somebody else probably had a green jacket. I myself didn't notice any camouflage uniforms, that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just focus for a while on Jeskovo. You said that you had seen a few members of the PJP. Can you tell me when did you see them exactly? I'm talking about Jeskovo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We saw members of the PJP somewhere in the middle of the village or halfway through the village while we were passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like again to see the document which is still on our screens, and I'm going to read to you what the international verifiers say. And it reads as follows: "Colonel Petrovic and the milicija entered Jeskovo in order to carry out an investigation into yesterday's VJ operations in the village." So we are talking about the 12th of March, which has been discussed the next day, and this claim states that this operation had been conducted by the VJ and that the police came only the next day to carry out an investigation. Would you allow for a possibility that the verifiers were right after all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that possibility because what one sees, one cannot deny because they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Milosevic case, do you remember mentioning members of the PJP in Jeskovo, or better yet, I'm going to put it to that you didn't. That was in 2002, which is to say three years after the event. Can you explain to us why this happened? How come the date suddenly appeared in 2006?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I cannot tell you for sure. That may have or may have not been the question, but I really don't remember. You can check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the mentioning of the PJP unit or does it have anything to do that you are giving evidence today against the general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the reason for your mentioning PJP in your today's evidence the fact that this is a trial of a police general and does it affect your testimony in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can only confirm what happened, and I don't know if there can be any other influence or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go on. I'll go back again to your statement and the next incident you mention. That next incident was in Trnje. And since the documents you spoke of have been admitted, I would like to call up these documents again and see what inferences you can make.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one is 65 ter 01981 or P1316.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at this document, Witness. Tell me, in the course of 1999, did you ever see that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You as a soldier in that period, did you ever have occasion to read an order like this? Would something like this ever be communicated to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We did not work in any positions in offices where these orders would pass through our hands. We would only receive orders in the field from our superiors, but of course we had no access to anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you look at this order, do you believe that certain military knowledge and training and education is needed to interpret this in the right way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: What could I know about that? The order is written for those who need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: But we will both agree that you are not one of those who need an order of this kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I haven't read it through. I can read it and then I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please do because you mention it in your statement. And while you read it, let me tell you what to pay special attention to. First of all, you say that items 5 and 6 of this order relate to the location allocated to the logistical battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make this as short as possible, can we ask the Legal Officer to show us items 5 and 6 in this document. I'll tell you the page. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this point 5.6? It says: "Forces to seal off territory."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can only recognise Trnje. These other features, I really don't know these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is your battalion mentioned anywhere in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise you answered my question. So you can't see your battalion anywhere in 5.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a Prosecution exhibit, P1317.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the document is shown on the screen, I'd like to discuss with you a couple of locations we saw in the previous document. Do you know what Jezera [phoen] feature is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Mistra feature is? I'm reading from para 5.6 which is the line to be sealed off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: What are these names, are they place names? I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Smuc [phoen] village tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really don't remember these names. I cannot remember all the place names in the territory we passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you don't know whether this 5.6 refers to the position of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: The only connection I can make with my battalion is the mention of Trnje village. I don't know any of these other features. I know that there is Lesane and Suva Reka and Mamusa in that area. The rest of these place names tell me nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now look at this exhibit on the screen. The question remains the same, did you have occasion in 1999 to see this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, as far as these documents are concerned, there was absolutely no chance that we would ever get to see documents like this. I told you so earlier. Nobody would show such things to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you mention and comment upon the paragraph that begins with the words "on the third day of combat operations..." Do you see it? It's towards the bottom. It says: "On the" -- it's the penultimate paragraph on the screen. "In the course of the third day of combat operations ..." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you claim that you did not see KLA members trying to pull out across that brook towards Trnje and Lesane villages. If we read this paragraph, we see this: "Part of the Siptar terrorist forces attempted to pull out along the creek to the villages of Trnje and Lesane." Am I right in saying that the word used is "attempted," which mean they did not succeed. And you are right in saying that you did not see them because they did not come across you, but since this was just an unsuccessful attempt, you can't claim that they did not try to pull out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, as I said in my statement, we could only see two persons trying to pass through, but that was after we had gone on top of that hill. And before that, if there had been any other people trying to withdraw, there's no chance that we wouldn't have seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Donje Retimlje village is? How far is it from Trnje, in which direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at that paragraph it says: "The mopping up operation of the main area around the village of Donje Retimlje was conducted." That's where the operation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I really don't understand in which direction Retimlje lies and how far it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, doesn't that mean that you couldn't possibly know where the Siptar terrorist forces attempted to pull out towards Trnje village, and by the same token, you cannot know whether you would have seen them or not because it doesn't say anywhere that they were close to Trnje village or that they had entered Trnje village, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: In my statement when I speak about this, I describe what happened where we were and what we came across. How could I possibly know what happened in the surrounding area and how could I know about all the things there? I am only speaking about the things in and around our location, things that I had seen. I cannot talk about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've reached a point in the evidence where it is convenient to have the second break, although it is a little later than usual. We will have the break now and resume at 5 minutes past 6.00. Again, for convenience and for -- in view of our orders for protective measures, we would now order that we go into private session and close the shutters. And the shutters will be closed when we resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us move on. Paragraph 17, 18 and 19, in which you speak about the crime that took place in a yard after you had entered the village of Trnje, and on which occasion about 15 Albanian civilians were killed. Is what I just stated correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I think you are right, only I'm not sure about the exact number, but thereabout.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that among these Albanian civilians, there were old men, women, and a woman with a baby, is that correct, as you stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you shoot at these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, I did shoot in their direction where this group was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How far away were you while you were shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. A few metres certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you what you said in paragraph 19 of your statement. You said, We were standing 1 to 2 metres from the group. So was that the distance that you were at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember. I don't know exactly how far I was, and I cannot remember that particular detail right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot remember now, but you could in 2006. If you were shooting from 1 or 2 metres, who were you shooting at? You couldn't have shot in the direction of those people within 1 or 2 metres, that was point-blank shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was 1 to 2 metres, I know that I was shooting in their direction. They were in front of us, and I really don't know the exact distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How many rounds did you fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe two short bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Here you said that it lasted 10 to 15 seconds. How many rounds did you fire during that period and which weapon did you use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I was shooting from an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And how many rounds can you fire from an automatic weapon in two bursts in 10 to 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Sir, this is not a constant fire. You fire two rounds, for instance, and then you move away.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This 1 or 2 rounds, how many bullets is that, more than 10? Can you fire fewer bullets from an automatic rifle in 10 to 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know about 10 to 15 seconds. That's how it lasted. That was while we were there. Probably that was the period. It wasn't a continuous fire within 10 to 15 seconds. It was not done by one person. It could have been 100 or more rounds. I know what I personally did and that I fired one or two short bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning that your statement is consistent with what happened on that date, so you were standing 1 to 2 metres from these people, you fired two bursts of rounds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, that's not what the statement says. It's speaking about a group of soldiers and a group of somewhere about 15 people. Now, inevitably they are going to be spread over a distance. And it says: "We were standing..." "we," being the soldiers, "were standing about 1 or 2 metres away from the group." Now, the figures are correct but the concept is not of a group of soldiers 1 metre or 2 metres from a group of 15 people. You've got to look at the picture as it is being fully described. And the whole incident which he describes as "it" lasted 10, 15 seconds. It is not being suggested by the witness that he fired for 10 to 15 seconds. So if you'd keep in mind what is actually in the statement as you put your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That was exactly what I am trying to clarify from the witness, and I'm going to try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So from the distance from which you were shooting at those people, do you know exactly who you were aiming at and whether there was a specific target that you have chosen? I'm referring to a specific person in the group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, there was no specific target because we were not firing from the shoulder, but from under our arm, so we just fired in the general direction of the group. At least that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware that it is not your duty to carry out unlawful orders, and that was such an order that you received from your sergeant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. On the contrary, it's always been said that those who refuse to obey orders during war-time can be sentenced to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That was the story that was circulating, but before the break you told us about the soldier who refused to kill a man and you saw for yourself that nothing bad happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: It didn't at that time, but as far as I know this sergeant never joined us in any action before that, as far as I can remember. So that means that only certain people were involved in those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: But you shouldn't have been afraid of any punishment because only minutes before that, as you told us yourself, a private refused to carry out an order and nothing happened to him. Why would you only minutes later fear that something would happen to you if you disobeyed an order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Sir, you probably don't know how a person feels at such moment, especially at that age and when you find yourself in such a situation. There were so many unpleasant situation in the army, starting from your superiors and the rest of it. If you disobey an order, I very much doubt that you can go unpunished.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So fearing that you would fare badly, you fired at those people even though only minutes before that you yourself witnessed that no punishment was pronounced against the person who refused to obey an order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I already explained this to you. And for me that was the only reason to remain there. There was no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness K82, am I right in saying that never an order was issued by anyone from among the ranks of your superior to shoot at those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean, that never an order of that nature was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean that you had never been given an order to shoot at these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: How could that be possible since we, who were standing there with our sergeant, were asked to come closer and carry out this order? How could you claim now that no such order had ever been issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that witness K54 described precisely this same event that you are talking about in the Milutinovic case and on that occasion he said that you personally told him that you were the one who killed this woman holding a baby in her arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: First of all, K54 was not there, therefore he could not have seen that. Secondly, this woman with the baby, there's no chance that I could have fired at her because she was to the far left and I was next to the sergeant, so there was no chance for me to shoot at her from that position. And I believe that is utter falsehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So we can conclude that K54 was telling untruths and that you never said anything of that nature to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever report to any authority the event that you took part in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: What do you mean by "authority"?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Any authority in Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: How was I to report that? Who was I going to go to at the state level and report the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't do that because you were afraid of being punished for that? Did you or were there any other reasons that prompted you not to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
